In [[statistics]], '''hierarchical generalized linear models''' extend [[generalized linear models]] by relaxing the assumption that [[Errors and residuals in statistics|error components]] are [[Independence (probability theory)|independent]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Generalized Linear Models|year=1989|publisher=Chapman and Hall/CRC|isbn=0-412-31760-5}}</ref> This allows models to be built in situations where more than one error term is necessary and also allows for dependencies between error terms.<ref name=paper1996 /> The error components can be [[Correlation and dependence|correlated]] and not necessarily follow a [[normal distribution]]. When there are different clusters, that is, groups of observations, the observations in the same cluster are correlated. In fact, they are positively correlated because observations in the same cluster share some common features. In this situation, using generalized linear models and ignoring the correlations may cause problems.<ref name=CDA>{{cite book|last=Agresti|first=Alan|title=Categorical Data Analysis|year=2002|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Inc.|location=Hoboken, New Jersey|isbn=0-471-36093-7}}</ref>

==Overview and model==

===Model===
In a hierarchical model, observations are grouped into clusters, and the distribution of an observation is determined not only by common structure among all clusters but also by the specific structure of the cluster where this observation belongs. So a random effect component, different for different clusters, is introduced into the model. Let <math>y</math> be the response, <math>u</math> be the random effect, <math>g</math> be the link function, <math>\eta = X \beta </math>, and <math>v = v(u)</math> is some strictly [[monotone function]] of <math>u</math>. In a hierarchical generalized linear model, the assumption on <math>y|u</math> and <math>u</math> need to be made:<ref name=paper1996 /> <math> 
y\mid u \sim\ f(\theta,\,\phi)
</math> and <math>
u \sim\ f_u(\alpha).
</math>

The linear predictor is in the form:

: <math>
g(E(y)) = g(\mu) = \eta = X \beta + v \,
</math>

where <math>g</math> is the link function, <math> \mu = E(y)  </math>,  <math> \eta = X \beta + v  </math>, and <math>v = v(u)</math> is a monotone function of <math>u</math>. In this hierarchical generalized linear model, the fixed effect is described by <math> \beta </math>, which is the same for all observations. The random component <math>u</math> is unobserved and varies among clusters randomly. So <math>v</math> takes the same value for observations in the same cluster and different values for observations in different clusters.<ref name=CDA />

===Identifiability===
[[Identifiability]] is a concept in [[statistics]]. In order to perform parameter inference, it is necessary to make sure that the identifiability property holds.<ref name=identifiability>{{cite journal |title=Identifiability of Parameters in Latent Structure Models with Many Observed Variables |journal=The Annals of Statistics|year=2009|volume= 37, No. 6A |pages=3099–3132 |arxiv=0809.5032 |bibcode=2008arXiv0809.5032A |last1=Allman |first1=Elizabeth S.|author1-link= Elizabeth S. Allman |last2=Matias |first2=Catherine |last3=Rhodes |first3=John A. |doi=10.1214/09-AOS689 |issue=6A|s2cid=16738108 }}</ref> In the model stated above, the location of v is not identifiable, since

: <math>
X \beta + v = (X \beta + a) + (v - a) \,
</math>

for constant <math>a</math>.<ref name=paper1996 /> In order to make the model identifiable, we need to impose constraints on parameters. The constraint is usually imposed on random effects, such as <math>E(v)=0</math>.<ref name=paper1996 />

===Models with different distributions and link functions===

By assuming different distributions of <math>y\mid u</math>  and <math>u</math>, and using different functions of <math>g</math> and '<math>v</math>, we will be able to obtain different models. Moreover, the [[generalized linear mixed model]] (GLMM) is a special case of the hierarchical generalized linear model. In hierarchical generalized linear models, the distributions of random effect <math>u</math> do not necessarily follow [[normal distribution]]. If the distribution of <math>u</math> is normal and the [[generalized linear model|link function]] of <math>v</math> is the [[identity function]], then hierarchical generalized linear model is the same as GLMM.<ref name=paper1996 />

Distributions of <math>y\mid u</math> and <math>u</math> can also be chosen to be conjugate, since nice properties hold and it is easier for computation and interpretation.<ref name=paper1996 /> For example, if the distribution of <math>y\mid u</math> is [[Poisson distribution|Poisson]] with certain mean, the distribution of <math>u</math> is [[Gamma distribution|Gamma]], and canonical log link is used, then we call the model Poisson conjugate hierarchical generalized linear models. If <math>y\mid u</math> follows [[binomial distribution]] with certain mean, <math>u</math> has the conjugate [[beta distribution]], and canonical logit link is used, then we call the model Beta conjugate model. Moreover, the mixed linear model is the normal conjugate hierarchical generalized linear models.<ref name=paper1996>{{cite journal|author1=Y. Lee|author2=J. A. Nelder|title=Hierarchical Generalized Linear Models|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B|year=1996|volume= 58| issue =  4|pages=619–678|doi=10.1111/j.2517-6161.1996.tb02105.x |jstor=2346105}}</ref>

==Fitting the hierarchical generalized linear models==
Hierarchical generalized linear models are used when observations come from different clusters. There are two types of estimators: fixed effect estimators and random effect estimators, corresponding to parameters in : <math>
\eta = \mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta
 </math> 
and in <math>
\mathbf{v(u)}
 </math>  , respectively. There are different ways to obtain parameter estimates for a hierarchical generalized linear model. If only fixed effect estimators are of interests, the population-averaged model can be used. If inference is focused on individuals, random effects will have to be predicted.<ref name=CDA /> There are different techniques to fit a hierarchical generalized linear model.

==Examples and applications==
Hierarchical generalized linear model have been used to solve different real-life problems.

===Engineering===
For example, this method was used to analyze semiconductor manufacturing, because interrelated processes form a complex hierarchy.<ref name=engg>{{cite journal|author1=Naveen Kumar |author2=Christina Mastrangelo |author3=Doug Montgomery |title=Hierarchical Modeling Using Generalized Linear Models|journal=Quality and Reliability Engineering International|year=2011}}</ref> [[Semiconductor fabrication]] is a complex process which requires different interrelated processes.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Chung Kwan Shin |author2=Sang Chan Park  |title=A machine learning approach to yield management in semiconductor manufacturing|journal=International Journal of Production Research |year=2000 |volume=38 |pages=4261–4271 |doi=10.1080/00207540050205073 |issue=17|s2cid=111295634 }}</ref> Hierarchical generalized linear model, requiring clustered data, is able to deal with complicated process. Engineers can use this model to find out and analyze important subprocesses, and at the same time, evaluate the influences of these subprocesses on final performance.<ref name=engg />

===Business===
[[Market research]] problems can also be analyzed by using hierarchical generalized linear models. Researchers applied the model to consumers within countries in order to solve problems in nested data structure in international marketing research.<ref name=mktresearch>{{cite journal |author1=Burcu Tasoluk |author2=Cornelia Dröge |author3=Roger J. Calantone |title=Interpreting interrelations across multiple levels in HGLM models: An application in international marketing research|journal=International Marketing Review|year=2011|volume= 28| issue =  1 |pages=34–56 |url=http://www.emeraldinsight.com/journals.htm?articleid=1911622&show=abstract|doi=10.1108/02651331111107099}}</ref>
